section_summary: This section follows U.S. concern over Japanese crab canning and trawling in the Bering Sea near Alaska during 1930–31. Commerce, State, the Coast Guard, and the embassy in Tokyo exchanged reports about the vessels, possible effects on salmon and halibut, and ways to regulate fishing beyond territorial waters. By February 1931, Japanese representatives said they did not expect to send a floating cannery to Alaska that year, chiefly because the previous season had been unprofitable.

subfiles.title: Japanese cannery operations in the Bering Sea
subfiles.about: Commerce reports Japanese crab fishing near Bristol Bay and warns of possible harm to American salmon and halibut fisheries.
subfiles.summary: The letter relays Coast Guard observations of the Taihoyu Maru and accompanying vessels off Port Moller. It raises concern about possible expansion from crab fishing to salmon or halibut and asks State to consider action if American fisheries are harmed.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Commerce’s July 8 letter
subfiles.about: State acknowledges the report and requests further information from its Tokyo embassy.
subfiles.summary: State has asked the Tokyo embassy to investigate the cannery company’s activities and plans.

subfiles.title: Inquiry to the Tokyo embassy
subfiles.from: Francis White, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: State sends Commerce’s report and asks about the Kokusai Floating Cannery Company.
subfiles.summary: Requests available information on the company’s activities and plans.

subfiles.title: Forwarding Coast Guard patrol reports
subfiles.about: Commerce forwards two reports on Japanese vessels near Alaska.
subfiles.summary: Notes that the Taihoyu Maru’s master refused to let a Coast Guard officer board.

subfiles.title: Follow-up patrol report on the Taihoyu Maru
subfiles.from: R. W. Dempwolf, Bering Sea Patrol Force
subfiles.about: The Chelan finds the floating cannery farther east and observes crab fishing.
subfiles.summary: The patrol saw crab catches but no evidence of fur sealing. It informed Bureau of Fisheries agent Dennis Winn and planned to continue observing the vessel.

subfiles.title: Messages about observing the floating cannery
subfiles.from: R. W. Dempwolf and Dennis Winn
subfiles.to: Dennis Winn and Coast Guard cutter Chelan
subfiles.about: The Chelan reports the cannery’s new position, and Winn agrees to observe it.
subfiles.summary: Two short messages exchange the cannery’s position and Winn’s promise to watch its activities.

subfiles.title: Initial patrol report on Japanese vessels
subfiles.from: R. W. Dempwolf, Bering Sea Patrol Force
subfiles.about: The patrol identifies the Taihoyu Maru and describes Japanese fishing and training vessels.
subfiles.summary: Dempwolf describes the Hakuyo Maru, the Taihoyu Maru, the Myogi Maru, and their activities near Baird Bank. The Taihoyu Maru was outside territorial waters; its master provided details but refused boarding. Dempwolf suspects the training ship helped locate commercial crab grounds.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of patrol reports
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: State acknowledges the reports and requests duplicate copies of future correspondence.
subfiles.summary: State has forwarded the reports to Tokyo and asks for duplicates of future letters and enclosures.

subfiles.title: Further reports sent to Tokyo
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: State sends the embassy Commerce’s July 23 letter and Coast Guard enclosures.
subfiles.summary: Forwards further evidence about the Japanese cannery’s Bering Sea activities.

subfiles.title: New position of Japanese fishing vessels
subfiles.about: Commerce relays a Coast Guard telegram locating the cannery and associated craft near Cape Kutuzof.
subfiles.summary: Reports that the vessels were catching and canning crabs about 23 miles off Cape Kutuzof.

subfiles.title: Embassy inquiry into Japanese crab fishing
subfiles.about: The embassy reports Japanese assurances that the floating cannery intends to catch crabs rather than salmon or halibut.
subfiles.summary: Foreign Office officials say Japanese interests are focused on crabs and will be warned away from areas where they might disrupt spawning salmon. Neville notes that other seafood is available closer to Japan.

subfiles.title: Embassy report forwarded to Commerce
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: State forwards Neville’s August 20 despatch.
subfiles.summary: Sends Commerce the embassy’s report on the Taihoku Maru.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese fishery budget
subfiles.about: The note points to another file on Japanese fishery spending and Soviet-water interests.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references a report on fishery subsidies, ports, whaling, and Soviet waters.

subfiles.title: Prospects for Japanese fishing in the Bering Sea
subfiles.about: Neville expects Japanese fishing to expand and proposes a comprehensive fishery treaty.
subfiles.summary: Improved refrigeration and canning could make distant Japanese fishing more profitable. Neville says voluntary warnings cannot control fishing beyond territorial waters and argues that coordinated treaty measures would be needed to protect salmon and halibut.

subfiles.title: Neville’s treaty proposal sent to Commerce
subfiles.about: State forwards Neville’s September 8 despatch for Commerce’s consideration.
subfiles.summary: Highlights Neville’s expectation of continued fishing and his proposal for a fishery treaty.

subfiles.title: Commerce requests detailed investigation
subfiles.about: Commerce asks the embassy to verify Japanese warnings and investigate catches, equipment, future plans, and reports of salmon canning.
subfiles.summary: Commerce seeks details on the Taihoku Maru and trawler Kakusai Maru, including a cautious inquiry into Seattle rumors of a large Japanese salmon pack. It emphasizes the value of Bristol Bay’s salmon fishery.

subfiles.title: Detailed inquiry requested from Tokyo
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: State asks the embassy for the detailed report requested by Commerce.
subfiles.summary: Forwards Commerce’s questions about the Taihoku Maru and Kokusai Maru.

subfiles.title: Reply to Commerce on embassy inquiry
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: State confirms its inquiry and explains the limits of Japanese control beyond territorial waters.
subfiles.summary: State has requested vessel details from Tokyo. It quotes Neville’s view that warnings alone cannot compel fishing vessels outside territorial waters and that a fishery treaty may be needed.

subfiles.title: Commerce’s assessment of Japanese crab fishing
subfiles.about: Commerce distinguishes relatively harmless offshore crab fishing from a potential threat to salmon runs.
subfiles.summary: Commerce sees no present reason to object if Japanese vessels remain offshore and catch crabs. It considers a treaty the likely remedy if they begin taking salmon, while recommending observation through the 1931 season.

subfiles.title: Commerce’s assessment sent to Tokyo
subfiles.about: State forwards Commerce’s October 4 letter.
subfiles.summary: Sends the ambassador Commerce’s assessment of Japanese fishing near Alaska.

subfiles.title: Fisheries conference memorandum sent to Tokyo
subfiles.about: State forwards a memorandum of discussion among U.S. fisheries, commerce, and State officials.
subfiles.summary: Sends the embassy a memorandum on Japanese fishing near Alaska.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Hokkaido salmon fishing
subfiles.about: The note points to an ambassadorial report concerning salmon fishing in Hokkaido.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Forbes’s comments on Hokkaido salmon fishing.

subfiles.title: Interdepartmental conversation on Japanese fishing
subfiles.about: U.S. officials discuss possible protections for Alaskan fisheries and concessions that might support negotiations with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Participants consider a treaty while recognizing that Japanese crab fishing poses little immediate competition. Possible concessions include changes to fur-seal arrangements and a lower duty on canned crab; O’Malley agrees to raise the matter with Commerce.

subfiles.title: Detailed embassy report on Japanese vessels
subfiles.about: The embassy identifies Japanese fishing vessels, their catches, licenses, and likely plans for the next season.
subfiles.summary: Forbes reports that the Taihoku Maru packed about 30,000 cases of crab and finds no support for rumors of a substantial salmon pack. He describes other trawlers and research vessels, Japanese licensing restrictions, and concern that fish-meal trawling could cause friction. He suggests informal discussions about tighter supervision.

subfiles.title: Possible informal regulation of Japanese fishing
subfiles.about: Forbes requests guidance for informal talks about Japanese fishing restrictions and possible concessions.
subfiles.summary: Japanese crab canners seek American cans and distribution arrangements, while American businesses want broader fishing rules. Forbes believes Japanese licenses could impose restrictions and asks what terms and concessions State would authorize. Pages 44–45 contain corrected and duplicate versions of the telegram’s second page.

subfiles.title: Interim reply to Forbes
subfiles.about: State says it is discussing Forbes’s proposal with Commerce.
subfiles.summary: Promises a fuller reply after consultation with Commerce.

subfiles.title: Internal recommendation for Commerce guidance
subfiles.about: The memorandum recommends asking Commerce to define needed protections and possible concessions.
subfiles.summary: Proposes obtaining Commerce’s position before instructing Tokyo to explore an agreement.

subfiles.title: Request for Commerce’s advice on Forbes’s telegram
subfiles.about: Castle seeks Commerce’s advice on fishing limits and conditions for Japanese operations.
subfiles.summary: Encloses Forbes’s telegram and the embassy’s January 12 report, asking what reply should be sent to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Handwritten State Department note
subfiles.about: A largely illegible handwritten note appears in the fisheries file.
subfiles.summary: The available OCR does not establish its substantive message.

subfiles.title: Handwritten Assistant Secretary note
subfiles.about: A largely illegible handwritten note appears on Assistant Secretary stationery.
subfiles.summary: The available OCR does not establish its substantive message.

subfiles.title: Request for proposed fishery protections
subfiles.about: Castle asks Commerce to specify protective measures and possible concessions before embassy talks.
subfiles.summary: Returning O’Malley’s memorandum, Castle requests an outline of practical protections for American fisheries and what the United States could offer Japan in return.

subfiles.title: O’Malley memorandum on Japanese vessels
subfiles.about: O’Malley warns that Japanese offshore fishing could undermine U.S. salmon conservation.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews Japanese vessels seen near Bristol Bay and the risk that high seas salmon fishing could defeat U.S. conservation measures. O’Malley suggests State consider treaty negotiations with Japan.

subfiles.title: Commerce’s proposed terms for Japanese fishing
subfiles.about: Commerce sets out its objections to Japanese fishing near Alaska and possible concessions.
subfiles.summary: Commerce opposes encouraging foreign fishing or allowing arrangements for cans and pack delivery in Alaska. It favors a lower canned-crab duty and would consider relinquishing U.S. fur-seal skins from Robben Island. It would prefer Japanese vessels to withdraw from the high seas off Alaska.

subfiles.title: Conference on draft reply to Tokyo
subfiles.about: State and Commerce officials review a draft response to the embassy’s fishing proposal.
subfiles.summary: The group approves an amended draft for formal Commerce review. Participants discuss authority for a crab-duty reduction, offshore transfer of cans and packed crab, and difficulties with reopening the fur-seal convention.

subfiles.title: Draft negotiating position for Tokyo
subfiles.about: The draft outlines proposed U.S. conditions and possible concessions concerning Japanese fishing.
subfiles.summary: It seeks continued Japanese limits on fishing near Alaska and suggests a crab-duty reduction in return. It rejects fishing in territorial waters, leaves arrangements for cans unresolved, and reserves a fur-seal concession as a possibility.

subfiles.title: Tariff authority reconsidered
subfiles.about: Officials question whether the proposed canned-crab duty reduction could be made under existing tariff law.
subfiles.summary: After checking the tariff provision, Moser concludes it likely cannot support the proposed reduction. Miller notes that this removes a possible bargaining point and informs O’Malley.

subfiles.title: Recent correspondence sent to Tokyo
subfiles.about: State forwards recent Commerce correspondence and two memoranda.
subfiles.summary: Supplies the embassy with the latest U.S. discussions on Japanese fishing.

subfiles.title: Japanese canners’ decision for 1931
subfiles.about: Japanese representatives say they will send no floating cannery to Alaska in 1931.
subfiles.summary: Unprofitable operations and competition lead the crab guild to defer its Alaska season.

subfiles.title: Embassy telegrams sent to Commerce
subfiles.about: State sends its February 6 telegram and the embassy’s February 9 reply to Commerce.
subfiles.summary: Requests Commerce’s comments on the exchanged telegrams.

subfiles.title: Crab guild approaches the embassy
subfiles.about: Japanese crab canners seek American supply and distribution arrangements and discuss possible fishing regulation.
subfiles.summary: Baron Iwakura says the prior crab-canning voyage lost money because supplies and grading required a return to Japan. Embassy official Dooman explains that American suppliers may want Japanese trawling regulated before cooperating. Iwakura agrees to seek an arrangement that protects Alaskan fisheries.

subfiles.title: Iwakura discusses licensing and trawlers
subfiles.about: Iwakura describes Japanese licensing powers and prospects for restricting trawlers near Alaska.
subfiles.summary: Iwakura says his guild might abandon Bristol Bay operations to avoid antagonizing American buyers. He believes Japanese authorities can impose and enforce license conditions acceptable to the United States, and provides a table of licensed trawler operators.

subfiles.title: Iwakura despatches sent to Commerce
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: State forwards the embassy’s January 23 and 27 despatches.
subfiles.summary: Sends Commerce both reports on Japanese fishing interests.

subfiles.title: Commerce response to Japanese decision
subfiles.about: Commerce welcomes the decision against a 1931 Japanese cannery voyage and requests further updates.
subfiles.summary: Commerce hopes Japanese fishing near Alaska will not resume and asks to hear the results of embassy discussions.

subfiles.title: Commerce response sent to Tokyo
subfiles.about: State forwards Commerce’s February 20 letter.
subfiles.summary: Sends Commerce’s reaction to Japanese fishing plans.

subfiles.title: Abstract of embassy despatch No. 134
subfiles.about: An internal summary describes the embassy’s meeting with Japanese officials and fishing representatives.
subfiles.summary: Notes losses from the 1930 crab pack, no planned 1931 guild voyage, and willingness to consider U.S. conditions.

subfiles.title: Informal meeting on Japanese fishing near Alaska
subfiles.about: Forbes reports a meeting on Japanese fishing methods, catches, and possible trawler regulation.
subfiles.summary: Japanese officials describe trawl nets, crab-net mesh, reported distances offshore, and the absence of a commercial salmon catch. Forbes stresses concern about interference with salmon runs and argues that regulating trawlers could help crab canners secure American distribution arrangements. The despatch continues beyond page 80.
